subject: Microsoft stopped renting Oracle's older Nvidia chips
bodyMarkdown:
A contract from 2023 going dark tells me more about the AI buildout than any earnings call this quarter. If you hold an index fund or a workplace pension, the two companies in this story are probably among your largest positions without you choosing them.

## What Microsoft switched off

Bloomberg reported on Friday that Microsoft is winding down an arrangement, signed in 2023, to rent AI computing capacity from Oracle. Microsoft declined to renew it and has spent recent months turning the capacity off. The reason, according to people Bloomberg spoke to, is that the servers run older generation Nvidia chips, and Microsoft's requirements have moved on, so the hardware no longer meets its specifications. The size of the contract, its pricing and its start and end dates were never disclosed, which makes the hole hard to measure from outside. Bloomberg placed the decision inside a wider review of billions of dollars of cloud partnerships, and noted that Microsoft has committed more than 80 billion US dollars to rent capacity from companies including CoreWeave, Nscale and Nebius. Microsoft is still buying compute at enormous scale. What it will not do is keep paying for an older vintage of it.

## How long is a GPU worth renting

That question sits under the entire AI capital spending boom, and Friday put a rough number on it. Oracle has borrowed heavily to buy chips and pour concrete, and that only works if a server keeps collecting rent for years after it is installed. The accounting term is **useful life**, the assumption a company makes about how long equipment keeps earning before it has to be written down, and it quietly supports every data centre projection you have read. Microsoft has now said with its chequebook that hardware from around 2023 does not meet the spec for the work it wants done in late 2026. I do not know whether that judgment extends to every older GPU or only to this one contract. Nobody outside these companies does, and that is the uncomfortable part.

## Oracle's answer, and the tape

Oracle pushed back the same day. It said demand for its AI infrastructure remains strong, including for earlier generation GPUs, and posted on X that older capacity coming up for renewal in its first quarter was renewed or resold at a 20 per cent premium to prior pricing on long term contracts, with most of the chips involved at least four years old. If that holds up, old silicon rents fine and Friday was noise. The tape disagreed. Oracle fell more than 4 per cent to a two year low, leaving the stock down more than half from its June 1 high of 248.15 US dollars. The report also landed a day after a rough Thursday for chipmakers, when Nvidia closed down 9.26 per cent at 181.60 before recovering 2.78 per cent on Friday.

## The takeaway

Oracle's next quarterly report is where I would look, and the first thing I will check is whether anything changes in how long the company assumes its servers keep earning. Watch for other tenants letting older capacity lapse without a press release, because one non renewal is a negotiation and a pattern of them is a repricing of the rental market that funds these builds. If you invest from Canada, the exposure runs through US tech weightings rather than anything listed in Toronto, so it is worth knowing what share of your equity sits in a handful of American names. Oracle says old chips still rent at a premium, and Microsoft just declined to pay it.
